title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
hook: someone hunts the whole house for the glasses on top of their head. Shankara asks how you can look for what you already have
carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: Shankara's preface, the I and the this, and silver that turned out to be shell. When did you catch an I am that wasn't quite true? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

Drawers are open. Couch cushions are on the floor. Someone has checked the car twice. Where are my glasses? And then a family member, trying not to laugh, points at the top of their head. The glasses were there the whole time. The searching was real, and it was also strange: you can't exactly find what you never lost, and you can't search for something you've never heard of. Shankara puts this puzzle at the start of the Brahma Sutra's very first line. Now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. Wait, he says. Is Brahman already known, or not? Either answer seems to stop the inquiry before it starts. Today, his way out.
screen: `CUSHIONS ON THE FLOOR.` → `THE GLASSES WERE ON YOUR HEAD.` → `KNOWN, OR NOT KNOWN?`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle in Shankara's own setup. If Brahman is already well known, why inquire? If it's wholly unknown, how could you even want to know it? You can't wish for what you have no idea of. His answer is quiet and surprising. Brahman is known, in a way, because it is the self of everyone. Nobody, he says, ever thinks, I am not. Everyone is sure that they are. So the bare fact is never in doubt. What's in doubt is what this self is. And there, he says, people disagree widely. He lists the views. Some take the self to be the body, alive and aware. Some say it's the senses. Some, the mind. Some, a flicker of awareness, new each moment. Some say there is a self that acts and enjoys, apart from the body. Some speak of a Lord, separate from the self. Shankara lays these out as the views he will answer, and he gives his own: the self is Brahman itself. He adds why it matters. If you take hold of a mistaken view without examining it, he says, you might miss the highest good. So the inquiry is worth the effort, and it should lean on reasoning that serves the Upanishads. Notice what that does to the word jnana. It isn't finding a new object, like finding a coin. It's closer to the glasses. On his reading, nobody ever lacks the self, only clarity about it. Other Vedanta schools honor the same opening line and say what the self is differently. Here we're letting Shankara speak.
screen: `KNOWN, OR UNKNOWN?` · `NOBODY THINKS: I AM NOT.` · `MANY VIEWS OF THE SELF.` · `NOT FINDING, BUT CLARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in the one thing you're sure of. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Notice that you are here. You don't need to prove it or name it. Then let the mind offer its labels, one at a time: this body, these senses, these thoughts. Let each one pass without deciding anything. Come back each time to the plain sense of being here, before any label. If you pray, you can offer that plain presence. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing. On Shankara's reading of the first line, not finding something new, but becoming clear about the self you never lacked. Today's word.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Today, the next time you search for something that was right there, let it remind you of the glasses. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students study Shankara's commentary on the first sutra with a teacher, and the question of what the self is runs through their reading, reflection and meditation.

fork.setup: someone says: if Brahman is already known, why study? and if it's unknown, how can you even want it? you're Shankara. what do you answer?
options: Brahman is completely unknown until you study.
the self is known to be, but what it is stays in doubt.
the question has no answer, so stop asking.
fork.reveal: Shankara says nobody thinks I am not, yet people disagree about what the self is. that's why the inquiry is needed.

original.note: Sanskrit: the wish to know, from the same root as jnana; the key word of the Brahma Sutra's first line.

trapdoor: what you thought: you inquire into something you don't know at all.
what it means: for Shankara, the self is known to exist; the inquiry is about what it truly is.
what a scholar hears: Shankara on 1.1.1, the self as known through the sense of I, and the list of rival views of the self he goes on to answer.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 1.1.1 (now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman)

Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.1 (is Brahman known or unknown; nobody thinks 'I am not'; the conflicting views of the self; a mistaken view may cost the highest good; reasoning that serves the Upanishads)

notes: Paraphrase of Shankara on 1.1.1: the known/unknown dilemma; the existence of Brahman known as the self of all ('everyone is conscious that the self exists, and never thinks I am not'); the list of views (body with intelligence, the senses, the internal organ, momentary cognition, the void, an agent and enjoyer, an enjoyer only, an omniscient Lord, the self of the enjoyer). The list here is shortened and leaves out the void and the closing items. Confirm wording and that no school is misrepresented.
The schools behind the listed views (Lokayata, Buddhist schools, Nyaya, Samkhya, Yoga) are deliberately not named, to avoid any sense of ranking another tradition. A Keeper may prefer to name them.
Glasses-on-the-head is a modern hook, not Shankara's image.
Original jijnasa: confirm Devanagari and the pronunciation guide.
Editor pass: 'You never lacked the self' (telling the listener) reworded as Shankara's view: 'on his reading, nobody ever lacks the self, only clarity about it'.
